title: Mass File Rename With High Entropy
summary: Mass file rename with high entropy detection identifies a single process rapidly modifying, renaming or extending the names of many files across one or more directories where the resulting names exhibit high character entropy and consistent suffix patterns, which is the observable fingerprint of automated data encryption for impact. The behaviour matters because it is one of the last chances to interrupt an intrusion before recovery becomes expensive: once the rewrite completes across servers and backups the organisation is reduced to restoring from offline copies. The telemetry required is file system auditing or endpoint file-operation telemetry that captures the acting process, the parent process, the original and resulting file names, the operation type and the directory, together with process creation records for identity and a time-series aggregation capability so that rate per minute can be computed rather than evaluated file by file. The signal survives common evasion because the operation is inherently bulk and inherently fast; even a deliberately throttled encryptor must rename or rewrite thousands of files within a short window to be effective, and slowing down enough to avoid rate thresholds extends the attack to an impractical duration. Directories excluded from encryption to preserve a ransom note still produce a distinctive cluster of untouched paths. The detection breaks down in practice because legitimate software performs bulk rename operations routinely: archive extraction, media transcoding pipelines, document management migrations, development build systems, and backup rotation all write or rename many files quickly. Distinguishing them requires examining name entropy, suffix uniformity, the presence of an accompanying note file, whether the process deleted or created recovery artefacts, and whether shadow copies or backup services were affected in the same window. Coverage gaps also arise where telemetry is sampled, where network attached storage does not forward file auditing, and where the target is a database file rewritten in place rather than renamed, which produces far fewer file events.
objectives: Describe the file-system event patterns that distinguish automated encryption from ordinary bulk processing.
Compute a per-process rename and write rate from file telemetry and choose thresholds that balance delay against detection.
Measure name entropy and suffix uniformity and explain why they distinguish encrypted output from archive extraction.
Correlate mass file modification with recovery inhibition activity such as deletion of local backup state or shadow copies.
Plan containment decisions including process termination versus host isolation and the effect of each on evidence quality.
Produce a written incident timeline for a ransomware event using file, process and service telemetry.

dataSources: Endpoint file operation telemetry capturing process, target path, operation type and resulting file name
Windows Security file system auditing events for object creation, rename and write operations on monitored shares
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing to identify the acting binary and its parent
Service control manager events recording unexpected stop of backup, database or volume shadow copy services
Storage and network share access logs showing distributed write bursts from a single host or account
logic: Aggregate file create, rename and write events by acting process and host into short rolling windows, then alert when a single process exceeds a rate baseline that is implausible for interactive work. Score the alert higher when the resulting file names share a uniform suffix, when their characters are unusually random, when the same process touched multiple directories or mapped drives, and when recovery related services stopped or their state was cleared within the same window. Lower the score when the process is a known archiving or build tool operating inside its expected working directory chain, and require human confirmation before automatic containment on hosts where such tooling is normal.
pseudoQuery:
title: Mass File Rename With High Entropy Names
id: det-mass-file-rename-entropy
status: training
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  bulk_rename:
    EventType:
      - rename
      - create
      - write
    # grouped by process and host
  rate_threshold:
    condition: count(distinct TargetFilename) by ProcessGuid > 300 within 10m
  high_entropy_names:
    TargetFilename|re: '\\[A-Za-z0-9]{8,}\\.(locked|enc|encrypted|crypt|[a-z0-9]{3,5})$'
  recovery_artefacts:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - 'RECOVER'
      - 'DECRYPT'
      - 'README'
  condition: bulk_rename and rate_threshold and (high_entropy_names or recovery_artefacts)
fields:
  - ProcessImage
  - ParentImage
  - User
  - TargetFilename
  - Computer
level: critical
falsePositives: Archive and compression tools expanding or creating large numbers of files inside an expected working directory
Media transcoding, rendering and image pipeline jobs that write thousands of uniformly named output files
Source control checkouts, build systems and package managers materialising dependency trees in bulk
Document management migrations, bulk renames by administrators and data classification tooling
Backup and synchronisation agents that stage, rename or rotate large file sets on a schedule
tuningNotes: Baseline the rename, create and write rate for every process family that routinely touches more than a few hundred files per window, and apply those baselines per host role so build servers are not compared against workstations. Do not suppress the alert entirely for such processes; instead downgrade to a low severity event that still records the activity so that a ransomware binary masquerading as a signed tool produces a visible anomaly. Tier thresholds by criticality so a database server or domain controller crossing a modest threshold pages immediately while a developer workstation requires a higher count, and always keep the entropy and recovery-artefact conditions as separate boosts rather than as prerequisites. Finally, verify that file telemetry covers network shares and mounted volumes, because a detection limited to local drives will miss the fastest spreading events.
